extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, probability, scientific method, and evidence evaluation (philosophers, statisticians, scientists, legal analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for calculating probabilities, inferring causes from observed effects, and judging when observed coincidences indicate law rather than chance. Emphasises the role of antecedent knowledge, causes versus mere frequency, and limits of applying averages to individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's definition of probability (equally possible cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability consists in reducing events to a number of cases equally possible (such that we are equally undecided), and the probability of an event is the ratio of the number of favourable cases to the number of all possible cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two prerequisites for this calculation: (1) that among several events one and only one must happen, and (2) that we have no reason to expect any one more than another. Equally probable assignments may be justified either by specific experiment, general experience, or deductively (e.g., symmetry in a coin). Use this only when those prerequisites hold; otherwise seek better data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as degree of warranted expectation (subjective to evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of an event is not a quality of the event but the degree of ground which we have for expecting it; it differs between persons and changes as evidence changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat probability as intrinsic to the event. Update probabilities when new evidence arrives (example: learning a person has terminal consumption drastically alters probability they will die within a year). This supports treating probability as conditional on present knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-indifference rule under ignorance and composite-event reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When entirely ignorant of the proportions among mutually exclusive outcomes, we may reasonably assign equal probability to each single outcome; but composite events (e.g., 'not-white') sum the probabilities of their constituent outcomes, so one can rationally prefer a composite over a single outcome (e.g., expect 'not-white' two-to-one against 'white' when three colours equally possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry/ignorance only for primitive equiprobability assignments; be aware that composite alternatives change odds. Beware that a slight ground for surmise (even a little evidence) vitiates the equal-indifference estimate and should shift you to use specific facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal/causal-frequency knowledge over raw empirical frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities deduced from knowledge of the causes (their comparative frequency or favourability) provide a more secure basis for expectation than probabilities derived solely from observed frequencies of the effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, ascend from effects to causes and estimate comparative frequencies of causes favourable vs unfavourable to the event. Small improvements in causal data usually yield more benefit than elaborate mathematical manipulation of poor frequency data. Example: box of balls — probability better grounded in local conditions (number/size) than mere counting of outcomes without cause knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of valid induction underlying probability calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations of chances rest upon inductions about relative frequencies; to be legitimate, the induction used to determine those frequencies must itself be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the induction that yields the empirical proportion (e.g., 'ten out of a hundred') is justified by sufficiently representative observations or causal understanding. Probabilistic fractions are meaningful only insofar as the underlying induction is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's Sixth Principle (probability of cause given effect — product rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an effect and several possible causes whose presence is unknown, the probability that the effect was produced by any one cause is proportional to the antecedent probability of that cause multiplied by the probability that the cause, if present, would have produced the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by computing prior (antecedent) probability of each cause and the likelihood (probability of effect given the cause); the posterior odds are proportional to the product of these. Examples given: Case I (causes equal in efficacy but different antecedent frequencies), Case II (equal antecedent frequencies but different efficacies), Case III (unequal in both). This is the foundational rule for reasoning from effects to causes (a Bayes-like rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chance-calculus to test whether coincidences are casual (1/m^n rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the probability of a particular casual coincidence is 1/m, the probability that the same coincidence repeats n times in succession by chance is 1/m^n (e.g., ace twice in a row is 1/6^2 = 1/36).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a rule to estimate how improbable a series of coincidences would be if accidental. To decide between chance and causation, compare this accidental probability with the antecedent probability of alternative causal explanations; often after enough repetitions the chance hypothesis becomes less probable than even a small possibility of unfairness or other cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-evidence rule for accepting unknown laws vs chance
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether a repeated coincidence indicates a law rather than accident, compare the observed excess of coincidences above what chance predicts with how uncommon such an accidental deviation would be; if the excess is sufficiently unlikely under chance, it is reasonable to accept causation as an empirical law (subject to further correction by experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise numerical comparison with antecedent probability of an unknown law is usually impossible; practical decision relies on whether the observed surplus over expected accidental coincidences is extremely unlikely. Repeatability and the possibility of reproducing the experiment strengthen the inference to causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of averages for individual-case inference (misuse in testimony and juries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Population averages protect expectations about masses but are of small value for any one individual instance unless individuals rarely deviate from the average; applying broad average-based probability to individual witnesses or jurors is often a misapplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate witnesses by their consistency, conduct under cross-examination, relation to interests/partialities, mental capacity, etc., rather than by a crude global ratio of truthful to untruthful statements. For juries, beware reasoning that simply increasing numbers will reduce error, since common causes of error or shared prejudices can affect many members simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on complex probability calculus when better observations are attainable
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying advanced probabilistic formulas, seek to obtain better specific knowledge (observations or causal information); modest improvements in data quality are more valuable than elaborate computation on poor data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common error: mathematicians apply formal formulas to poorly founded data (e.g., witness credibility) instead of improving the observational basis. Prioritise collecting relevant facts and causal understanding before heavy calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws have narrower generality and depend on collocation of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (relations between effects derived from different primeval causes) are less generally true and less certain than ultimate laws; they often hold only where the same collocation of primeval causes exists and may fail when collocation varies or counteracting causes intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend empirical derivative laws beyond the time/place/conditions in which their collocations have been confirmed by observation. When extending to adjacent cases, verify that the necessary causes exist and are not counteracted. Example: day and night are derivative uniformities dependent on specific combination of sun, rotation, and observer; change collocation and the uniformity can fail.
